query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor alloying addition that segregates to the lamellar colony boundaries will enhance interfacial cohesion, thereby simultaneously increasing room‐temperature tensile strength and ductility relative to the conventional dual‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that contain numerous internal boundaries prone to microcracking under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Addition of a trace/minor alloying element (via, e.g., low-level doping) followed by a heat-treatment designed to promote segregation of this element to the lamellar colony interfaces.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing on samples processed under identical thermal histories, with an optimal range of minor element concentration to avoid forming deleterious secondary phases.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced cohesion at the lamellar colony interfaces through segregation of the minor element.
generation.mechanism: The minor element preferentially segregates to the interfaces between lamellar colonies, reducing interfacial free energy and suppressing microcrack initiation. This cohesive strengthening mechanism not only impedes crack propagation but also maintains or enhances dislocation-driven work hardening, leading to improved tensile strength and ductility simultaneously.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, samples treated with the minor alloying addition will exhibit higher tensile strength and greater tensile elongation, indicating improved ductility.
generation.baseline: The conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy processed without the targeted alloying addition exhibits high strength but limited ductility and brittle failure due to microcrack formation along weak lamellar interfaces.
generation.boundary: This strategy is expected to be effective only within a limited range of minor element concentration; excessive addition may lead to unwanted secondary phase formation or embrittlement. The mechanism is also most applicable under room-temperature tensile deformations where boundary-mediated cracking is a critical failure mode.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration and precise segregation kinetics of the alloying element require further experimental calibration. Moreover, the universality of the effect across varying alloy chemistries and processing conditions remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples with incremental additions of the minor alloying element (including a no-addition control group). Subject all samples to the same homogenizing heat treatment to facilitate segregation. Perform standard room-temperature tensile tests, supplemented by microstructural analyses such as high-resolution electron microscopy and elemental mapping to verify the segregation at interfaces.
measurements: Fractography to characterize crack formation and propagation
Elemental distribution at lamellar colony boundaries (via EDS or atom probe tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if samples with the minor alloying addition do not show a statistically significant simultaneous improvement in both tensile strength and ductility compared with the no-addition control, or if segregation of the alloying element at the lamellar boundaries cannot be confirmed by microstructural analysis.
